intelligence.human_view: A double-up is a clone sitting just behind the thing, offset by a hair, so the eye reads depth — one object sitting on another, a real thing with a shadow of itself. Move it a little too far and the trick breaks: now you SEE the spacing, you see two things with a gap between them, and the eye reads it as a mistake, not as depth. It looks weird. It doesn't look pro. The calibration is not a number you measure — it's a feeling you check with the eye: can you feel the depth? Can you see the gap? If you can see the gap, you went over much — pull it back until the gap disappears and only the depth is left. Just a tad. That is the whole law: the offset is a hair, never a step.
intelligence.simple_view: Imagine you draw a picture and then draw it again just a tiny bit behind it — so tiny you can hardly see it moved at all! That's what makes it look deep and real, like a real thing! But if you move the second picture too far — now you can SEE the space between them, and it looks weird and messy! So you only move it JUST A TAD — a tiny tiny bit — so you feel the depth but you never see the gap!
intelligence.grandma_view: It's like this, love — imagine you put a picture just behind itself, dear, moved over by the tiniest little bit — so small you can hardly see it! That's what makes it look deep and real, love, like a real thing sitting there! But if you move it too far, dear — now you can SEE the space between them, and it looks wrong, not professional at all! So you only move it just a tad, love — a hair — so you feel the depth but you never see the gap!
intelligence.naya_view: The double-up offset is a HAIR: feel the depth, never see the gap. Move too much and the spacing shows — it reads as a mistake, not as depth, and it doesn't look pro. "Just a tad" is the calibration, judged by the eye, not by measurement. Headline item of fix-4.
